newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian opposition outraged as poll win cancelled.
newsitem.headline: Serbian opposition outraged as poll win cancelled.

text.p: Authorities on Sunday annulled an opposition election victory in the capital Belgrade, provoking outrage in the anti-government coalition.
Leaders of the three-party opposition coalition said the decision showed the ruling Socialists led by President Slobodan Milosevic were making a mockery of the democratic process.
"This is proof that power cannot be won in Serbia by elections, that power is won by robbery," Zoran Djindjic, one of the Zajedno (Together) coalition leaders, told Reuters.

"We have now been brought to a dramatic situation in which all citizens are becoming aware that the regime in Serbia cannot be changed by elections and cannot be changed legally but only in another way -- illegally, by uprisings, strikes, violence."
A municipal court annulled 33 of 60 city council seats which were previously verified as won by the opposition in local elections a week ago, lawyers for the Zajedno coalition said.
The ruling, which state media had yet to confirm, stripped Zajedno of a majority in the 110-seat city council. Authorities had previously annulled 10 seats won by the Zajedno coalition.
Opposition officials retracted an earlier report saying the court had cancelled a higher number of seats.
Before Sunday, courts and electoral commissions had already cancelled opposition victories in the country's largest towns, citing alleged irregularities.

The opposition, accusing the authorities of massive fraud, has organised peaceful demonstrations in Belgrade and other towns over the past five days in the country's biggest street protests in three years.
The outcome of the local elections shocked the Socialists and has set off a major confrontation between the opposition and Milosevic, who has ruled Serbia with supreme authority for nine years.
The opposition says the local poll has punctured Milosevic's aura of invincibility. But the court ruling raised the stakes in the standoff and left the opposition with few options.
With Milosevic controlling a vast police force and the state media, the opposition was calling for strikes and civil disobedience.
Opposition leaders have appealed for international support, which they said could tip the balance in their favour.
But Western countries have so far offered only muted statements, expressing concern over possible election fraud.

The United States and European powers once accused Milosevic of igniting four years of war in former Yugoslavia. But they now view him as a guarantor of peace after he signed a U.S.-brokered peace treaty last year and may choose to give him a free hand at home.
Senior American and European diplomats on Saturday met Yugoslav foreign minister Milan Milutinovic to discuss the situation but declined to discuss details of the talks.

Local electoral authorities refused to comment to reporters but have already announced another round of voting on Wednesday in Belgrade. Opposition leaders said they would refuse to participate in another round of voting.
Some 20,000 supporters marched through the city centre on Sunday afternoon in a protest scheduled before the court's decision was announced.
Braving a light snowfall, the crowd cheered speakers who called for pressing ahead with the protests.
Zajedno says it won 70 seats in the 110-seat city council to capture the capital in run-off polls in an unprecedented defeat for Milosevic.
In towns where the opposition said it prevailed, local electoral commissions have either failed to announce final results or annulled results or ordered another round of voting.
